I am 76 years old and have been farming this land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I only finished primary school, but I have worked these fields for over 50 years, and I know the soil and the weather here better than any book. My family has about 6 mu of flat, good-quality land on the North China Plain. I thought about renting some of it out because my back is not what it used to be, but farming is my life, and 6 mu is just enough that I can manage it myself without exhausting my body.

This year, I will stick to what has always worked: I will plant **winter wheat** on all 6 mu this autumn, and after the wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately sow **summer maize** on the same land. I am too old to gamble with new crops like vegetables or melons — the wheat gives us flour for our own bread and noodles, and the maize is easy to sell at the grain station or to the feed mill. This rotation is what every neighbor around me does, and it has never let us go hungry.

For the wheat, I will **rotary-till** the field before sowing in early October. I will use an **improved wheat variety** — probably around 30 jin of seed per mu, the same kind my neighbors are planting. I will spread compound fertilizer as a basal dressing at sowing, and then topdress with urea in the spring when the wheat starts greening up. I will irrigate **four times**: once before winter to protect the seedlings from the cold, and then three more times in the spring at jointing, heading, and grain-filling. I will spray for weeds once, insects twice, and leaf diseases once or twice depending on whether the spring is humid. If the weather is normal, I expect to harvest around **1,050 jin per mu**.

For the maize, I will sow it right after the wheat is threshed in mid-June. There is no time to plough, and there is no need — I will use **no-tillage** sowing directly into the wheat stubble. I will buy **hybrid maize seed** from the county seed station, about one package per mu. I will apply compound fertilizer when I sow, and maybe a bit more urea when the plants are knee-high. Maize does not need as much water as wheat in our area — **two irrigations** are enough, one when the seedlings are small and one at the big trumpet stage. I will spray for insects, weeds, and leaf blight about **five times** in total. If there is no big drought or flood, I should get about **1,100 jin per mu**.

I will do most of the work myself, though I may hire the rotary tiller and the combine harvester from the village cooperative, and my son sometimes helps when he comes back from the city during busy seasons.
